Langman's Paradox

ParadoxesSequencesInvariants
Game: The same three pieces fill a Fibonacci square and a slightly different rectangle.
How to play: Change the Fibonacci size, and use Cheat to exaggerate the sliver hiding the missing unit.

The square

The rectangle

Look for the math

Dr. Harry Langman's dissection makes a square appear to become a rectangle of different area. The pieces never change size.

Fibonacci dimensions

The square has side F(n); the rectangle has sides F(n−1) and F(n+1). By Cassini's identity their areas differ by exactly one unit: F(n)² − F(n−1)F(n+1) = (−1)ⁿ. That missing or extra square is what the illusion hides.

The sloping join

The cut in the square has slope based on 3 and 5, while the rectangle pretends it is based on 5 and 8. The slopes differ slightly, so a thin sliver opens along the join. The logic test uses the shoelace formula for n = 4 through 12: the pieces always conserve area and the discrepancy is always one. The Cheat box widens the sliver visually without changing any piece.

Switch Cheat on and off. Does the number in the readout change?
